paper_metadata.title: Microstructure evolution and fracture mechanism of Mo/Cu alloyed interface during plastic deformation
paper_metadata.journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

evidence.quote: Microstructure evolution and fracture mechanism of Mo/Cu alloyed interface during plastic deformation
In this study, the Mo/Cu alloyed interfaces obtained by high-temperature and electric-field alloying process were subjected to loading in both vertical and parallel interface modes via MD simulation

evidence.section: 3.1 The microstructure of the alloyed interface
evidence.quote: the electric-field alloyed interface

The shearing process of the electric-field alloyed interface model was visualized and analyzed, with the evolution of the internal interface structure determined through CNA and DXA. The results are presented in Fig. 12 . In the initial state ( ε = 0), Mo contains perfect dislocations a / 2 < 111 > and a < 100 > , while Cu exhibits dislocation loops composed of Shockley dislocations, Stair-rod dislocations, and Hirth dislocations.
The initial model underwent a 0.8 ns relaxation process to fully release the internal energy of the system.
the holding temperature of 1200 K and a holding duration of 5 ns. Under these high-temperature conditions, complete atomic diffusion occurred, forming a high-temperature alloyed interface

When loaded parallel to the interface, the fixed rigid atomic layers move along the positive y-axis direction, resulting in deformation of the model box along the y and z axes.

For the high-temperature alloyed interface, the maximum stress of 5.18 GPa is reached at a strain of 0.034.

In contrast, the electric-field alloyed interface achieves a peak stress of 5.51 GPa at a strain rate of 0.037, which represents an approximately 6.4 % higher value compared to the high-temperature alloyed interface model.

due to the significant difference in atomic arrangement between the amorphous interface and the FCC structure of Cu, a potential barrier forms, preventing dislocations from crossing the amorphous interface. This leads to dislocation pile-up at the interface, causing severe stress concentration.
Severe dislocation pile-up at the interface triggers brittle fracture and interface failure.

The applied electric field accelerates processes such as dislocation slip, reaction, and annihilation, resulting in extensive dislocation annihilation within the interface and a more uniform stress distribution at the interface.
the electric field effectively reduces dislocation density within the interface, promoting a more uniform stress distribution at the interface.
Both locking structures play identical roles, enhancing the work hardening ability through the pinning effect of the central dislocations.
